## Where we are

- Last time: how to estimate a tree. Its branch lengths are in **substitutions/site** — a
  product of **rate × time**.
- To get a **timescale** (millions of years) we must separate rate from time — the central
  problem of **molecular dating**.
- **Today:** the molecular clock, relaxed clocks, calibration, and tree priors.

## Learning objectives

By the end you should be able to:

- State the **molecular clock** hypothesis and why $k=\mu$ makes it plausible.
- Explain why branch length **confounds rate and time**, and how **calibrations** break it.
- Contrast **strict** and **relaxed** clocks.
- Describe the **birth–death** tree prior and read a dated tree with its **HPD** intervals.

# The molecular clock {.center}

## Rate × time

A branch length in substitutions per site is

$$
b = r \times t \quad(\text{rate} \times \text{time}).
$$

The **molecular clock** hypothesis: $r$ is roughly constant across lineages, so branch
lengths are proportional to time.

::: {.callout-note}
Why is a clock even plausible? Recall the **neutral theory** (popgen deck 04): the neutral
substitution rate $k=\mu$ is **independent of population size**. If $\mu$ is similar across
lineages, molecular divergence ticks at a roughly constant rate.
:::

## Rate–time non-identifiability

From sequence data we observe only the **product** $b=rt$. Doubling the rate and halving the
time gives the *identical* likelihood:

$$
b = r\,t = (2r)\left(\tfrac{t}{2}\right).
$$

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- **Molecular data alone cannot date a tree.** We need **external time information**.
- This is exactly what the RevBayes practical demonstrates: an *uncalibrated* analysis
  returns wildly uncertain node ages.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.figure-prompt}

long time); two trees, identical topology and branch lengths, different axes.

## Calibrations break the tie

External evidence fixes ages (or age *distributions*) at nodes/tips:

- **Fossils** — a dated fossil places a *minimum* age on a clade (often a soft prior).
- **Secondary calibrations** — ages from a previous dated study.
- **Biogeographic** — island emergence, vicariance events (e.g. Hawaiian island ages).

::: {.callout-important}
Calibrations are **priors on time**, layered onto the rate–time product. Their choice and
placement dominate the resulting ages — report them explicitly.
:::

# Clock models {.center}

## Strict vs. relaxed clocks

- **Strict clock:** one rate $r$ for the whole tree. Simple, but real lineages vary (life
  history, generation time, mutation rate).
- **Relaxed clock:** each branch draws its own rate, e.g. from a **lognormal**:

$$
r_i \sim \text{Lognormal}(\mu_r, \sigma_r),
$$

with $\sigma_r$ measuring how **clock-like** the data are [@drummond2006].

- Uncorrelated (branch rates independent) vs. autocorrelated (parent→child) variants.
- Plants often violate a strict clock — herbs vs. trees differ in substitution rate.

## Tree priors: the birth–death process

Dating needs a **prior on the tree** (topology + node times). The standard is the
**birth–death process** with speciation $\lambda$ and extinction $\mu$:

$$
\text{net diversification } r = \lambda - \mu,\qquad
\text{turnover } \epsilon = \mu/\lambda.
$$

- The **Yule** process is the pure-birth special case ($\mu=0$).
- Incomplete sampling is handled by a sampling fraction $\rho$.

<span class="xref">→ the same birth–death process reappears as a *diversification model*
in the macroevolution module.</span>

## Fossilized birth–death (a note)

- The **fossilized birth–death (FBD)** process treats fossils as **sampled ancestors** on
  the same birth–death tree — unifying the tree prior and calibration.
- Enables **tip-dating** (fossils as dated tips) instead of ad hoc node calibrations.
- Powerful for plants with a rich (if patchy) macro- and micro-fossil record (pollen!).

# Reading a dated tree {.center}

## Bayesian divergence-time estimation

Put it together in one hierarchical model, sampled by MCMC:

$$
\underbrace{P(\text{data}\mid \tau, t, r)}_{\text{substitution + clock}}
\;\times\;
\underbrace{P(\tau, t)}_{\text{tree prior}}
\;\times\;
\underbrace{P(\text{calibrations})}_{\text{time priors}}.
$$

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}
- Output: a posterior distribution of **time-calibrated trees**.
- Every node age has a **95% HPD interval** — often wide. Report it; don't quote point ages
  alone.
:::

::: {.column width="45%"}
::: {.figure-prompt}
**FIGURE** — a time-calibrated tree with node bars (95% HPD) and a geological time axis;
Hawaiian *Kadua* or an angiosperm chronogram.

## Summary

- Branch length = **rate × time**; the two are **non-identifiable** from sequences alone.
- **Calibrations** (fossils, secondary, biogeographic) supply the time information.
- **Relaxed clocks** model rate variation; the **birth–death** process is the tree prior.
- Dating yields a **posterior of chronograms** — always with **HPD** uncertainty.
- <span class="xref">→ RevBayes molecular-dating practical: build an (un)calibrated analysis
  on *Kadua* and see the node-age uncertainty for yourself.</span>
